content.text:
1	---
     2	name: pdf-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when you need to read, inspect, or extract content from PDF files — especially when file content is NOT in your context and you need to read it from disk. Covers content inventory, text extraction, page rasterization for visual inspection, embedded image/attachment/table/form-field extraction, and choosing the right reading strategy for different document types (text-heavy, scanned, slide-decks, forms, data-heavy). Do NOT use this skill for PDF creation, form filling, merging, splitting, watermarking, or encryption — use the pdf skill instead."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# PDF Processing Guide
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	This guide covers essential PDF reading operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features (pypdfium2 rendering, pdfplumber table settings, OCR fallback, encrypted/corrupted PDF handling), see REFERENCE.md.
    12	
    13	## Reading & Inspecting PDFs
    14	
    15	Before doing anything with a PDF, understand what you're working with.
    16	
    17	### Content inventory
    18	
    19	Run a quick diagnostic first. For simple tasks ("summarize this
    20	document"), `pdfinfo` + a text sample may suffice. For anything
    21	involving figures, attachments, or extraction issues, run the full set:
    22	
    23	```bash
    24	# Always: page count, file size, PDF version, metadata
    25	pdfinfo document.pdf
    26	
    27	# Always: quick text extraction check — is this a text PDF or a scan?
    28	pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 document.pdf - | head -20
    29	
    30	# If figures/charts may matter:
    31	pdfimages -list document.pdf
    32	
    33	# If the PDF might contain embedded files (reports, portfolios):
    34	pdfdetach -list document.pdf
    35	
    36	# If text extraction looks garbled:
    37	pdffonts document.pdf
    38	```
    39	
    40	This tells you:
    41	- **Page count and size** — how big is the job?
    42	- **Text extractability** — does `pdftotext` return real text, or is
    43	  it empty (scanned) or garbled (broken font encoding)?
    44	- **Embedded raster images** — are there photos or raster figures?
    45	  (Note: vector-drawn charts from matplotlib/Excel won't appear — see
    46	  "Extracting embedded images" below)
    47	- **Attachments** — are there embedded spreadsheets, data files, etc.?
    48	- **Font status** — are fonts embedded? If not, text extraction may
    49	  produce wrong characters.
    50	
    51	### Text extraction
    52	
    53	**pypdf** for basic text:
    54	```python
    55	from pypdf import PdfReader
    56	
    57	reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
    58	print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")
    59	
    60	# Extract text
    61	text = ""
    62	for page in reader.pages:
    63	    text += page.extract_text()
    64	```
    65	
    66	**pdftotext** preserving layout (better for multi-column docs):
    67	```bash
    68	# Layout mode preserves spatial positioning
    69	pdftotext -layout document.pdf output.txt
    70	
    71	# Specific page range
    72	pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 document.pdf output.txt
    73	```
    74	
    75	**pdfplumber** for layout-aware extraction with positioning data:
    76	```python
    77	import pdfplumber
    78	
    79	with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    80	    for page in pdf.pages:
    81	        text = page.extract_text()
    82	        print(text)
    83	```
    84	
    85	### Visual inspection (rasterize pages)
    86	
    87	Text extraction is **blind** to charts, diagrams, figures, equations,
    88	multi-column layout, and form structures. When any of these matter,
    89	rasterize the relevant page and Read the image:
    90	
    91	```bash
    92	# Rasterize a single page (page 3 here) at 150 DPI
    93	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f 3 -l 3 document.pdf /tmp/page
    94	
    95	# pdftoppm zero-pads the output filename based on TOTAL page count
    96	# (e.g., page-03.jpg for a 50-page PDF, page-003.jpg for 200+ pages)
    97	# Don't guess the filename — find it:
    98	ls /tmp/page-*.jpg
    99	```
   100	
   101	Then Read the resulting image file. This gives you full visual
   102	understanding of that page — layout, charts, equations, everything.
   103	
   104	**When to rasterize vs. text-extract:**
   105	- **Content/data questions → text extraction** (cheaper, searchable)
   106	- **Figures, charts, visual layout → rasterize the page**
   107	- **Tables → try text extraction first, rasterize if garbled**
   108	- **Precision matters → do both** (extract text AND rasterize; use text
   109	  for data, image for context — this is what Claude's API does natively
   110	  with PDF uploads)
   111	
   112	**Token cost awareness:**
   113	- Text extraction: ~200–400 tokens per page
   114	- Rasterized image: ~1,600 tokens per page (at 150 DPI)
   115	- Both together: ~2,000–2,400 tokens per page
   116	
   117	For a 100-page PDF, rasterizing everything would consume ~160K tokens.
   118	Only rasterize pages that matter for the question at hand.
   119	
   120	### Choosing your reading strategy
   121	
   122	**Text-heavy documents** (reports, articles, books):
   123	→ Text extraction is primary. Rasterize only for specific figures or
   124	  pages where layout matters.
   125	
   126	**Scanned documents** (no extractable text):
   127	→ Rasterize pages at 150 DPI and Read them visually. For bulk text
   128	  extraction, use OCR (pytesseract after converting pages to images —
   129	  see REFERENCE.md for a complete example).
   130	
   131	**Slide-deck PDFs** (exported presentations):
   132	→ Every page is primarily visual. Rasterize individual pages on demand.
   133	  Text extraction gives you bullet-point text but loses all layout.
   134	
   135	**Form-heavy documents**:
   136	→ Extract form field values programmatically first (see below). Rasterize
   137	  the form page for visual context if needed.
   138	
   139	**Data-heavy documents** (tables, charts, figures):
   140	→ Use pdfplumber for tables. Rasterize pages with charts/figures.
   141	  Extract text for surrounding narrative. Consider both text AND image
   142	  for the same page when precision matters.
   143	
   144	### Extracting embedded images
   145	
   146	```bash
   147	# List all embedded images with metadata (size, color, compression)
   148	pdfimages -list document.pdf
   149	
   150	# Extract all images as PNG
   151	pdfimages -png document.pdf /tmp/img
   152	
   153	# Extract from specific pages only (pages 3-5)
   154	pdfimages -png -f 3 -l 5 document.pdf /tmp/img
   155	
   156	# Extract in original format (JPEG stays JPEG, etc.)
   157	pdfimages -all document.pdf /tmp/img
   158	```
   159	
   160	Then Read `/tmp/img-000.png` (etc.) to see each extracted image.
   161	
   162	**Gotcha — vector graphics:** `pdfimages` extracts only raster image
   163	data. Charts and diagrams drawn as vector graphics (common in
   164	matplotlib, Excel, and R exports) will NOT appear — they are page
   165	content operators, not image objects. For these, rasterize the whole
   166	page with `pdftoppm` instead.
   167	
   168	**Gotcha — empty images:** `pdfimages` sometimes produces many tiny or
   169	empty image files — these are typically background masks, transparency
   170	layers, or decorative elements. Filter by file size to find the real
   171	content images.
   172	
   173	Programmatic extraction with position data:
   174	```python
   175	import fitz  # PyMuPDF
   176	
   177	doc = fitz.open("document.pdf")
   178	for page in doc:
   179	    for img in page.get_images():
   180	        xref = img[0]
   181	        pix = fitz.Pixmap(doc, xref)
   182	        if pix.n - pix.alpha > 3:  # CMYK or other non-RGB
   183	            pix = fitz.Pixmap(fitz.csRGB, pix)
   184	        pix.save(f"/tmp/img_{xref}.png")
   185	```
   186	
   187	### Extracting file attachments
   188	
   189	PDFs can contain embedded files — spreadsheets, data files, other
   190	documents. Common in business reports, PDF portfolios, and PDF/A-3
   191	compliance documents.
   192	
   193	```bash
   194	# List all attachments
   195	pdfdetach -list document.pdf
   196	
   197	# Extract all attachments to a directory
   198	mkdir -p /tmp/attachments
   199	pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/attachments/ document.pdf
   200	
   201	# Extract a specific attachment by number (1-based index from -list output)
   202	pdfdetach -save 1 -o /tmp/attachment.pdf document.pdf
   203	```
   204	
   205	In Python:
   206	```python
   207	import os
   208	from pypdf import PdfReader
   209	
   210	reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
   211	for name, content_list in reader.attachments.items():
   212	    safe_name = os.path.basename(name)  # sanitize — name comes from the PDF
   213	    for content in content_list:
   214	        with open(f"/tmp/{safe_name}", "wb") as f:
   215	            f.write(content)
   216	```
   217	
   218	**Two attachment mechanisms exist in PDFs:** page-level file annotation
   219	attachments (shown as paperclip icons in viewers) and document-level
   220	embedded files (in the EmbeddedFiles name tree). Both `pdfdetach` and
   221	pypdf handle the common cases. Rich media assets (3D, video) embedded
   222	as annotations may not appear in the attachment list — use PyMuPDF to
   223	iterate page annotations for those.
   224	
   225	### Extracting form field data
   226	
   227	PDFs with interactive forms (government forms, applications, contracts)
   228	have fillable fields whose values can be read programmatically:
   229	
   230	```python
   231	from pypdf import PdfReader
   232	
   233	reader = PdfReader("form.pdf")
   234	
   235	# Text input fields only:
   236	fields = reader.get_form_text_fields()
   237	for name, value in fields.items():
   238	    print(f"{name}: {value}")
   239	
   240	# All field types (checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns too):
   241	all_fields = reader.get_fields() or {}
   242	for name, field in all_fields.items():
   243	    print(f"{name}: {field.get('/V', '')} (type: {field.get('/FT', '')})")
   244	```
   245	
   246	`get_form_text_fields()` returns only text input fields. For
   247	government forms and contracts that use checkboxes, radio buttons,
   248	and dropdowns, use `get_fields()` instead to see all field types.
   249	
   250	For comprehensive field info (types, options, defaults):
   251	```bash
   252	pdftk form.pdf dump_data_fields
   253	```
   254	
   255	For anything beyond reading form data — filling forms, creating forms —
   256	use the pdf skill at `/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   257	
   258	### Audio, video, and other rare embedded content
   259	
   260	PDFs can occasionally embed audio, video, or 3D models. Check
   261	`pdfdetach -list` first — if the media appears as an attachment,
   262	extract with `pdfdetach -saveall`. If not, it may be a Rich Media
   263	annotation (harder to extract; requires PyMuPDF to iterate page
   264	annotations). This is very rare in practice. Most PDF viewers outside
   265	Adobe Acrobat do not support media playback.
   266	
   267	### Font diagnostics
   268	
   269	If text extraction produces garbled output (wrong characters, missing
   270	text, mojibake), check the font situation:
   271	
   272	```bash
   273	pdffonts document.pdf
   274	```
   275	
   276	Look at the "emb" column — if fonts show "no" (not embedded) with
   277	custom encodings, the PDF's character mapping may be broken for text
   278	extraction. In that case, rasterize the page and use vision instead.
   279	
   280	Also check encoding: fonts with "Custom" or "Identity-H" encoding
   281	without embedded CIDToGID maps can cause character substitution issues
   282	even when the font is technically embedded.
   283	
   284	---
   285	
   286	## Quick Reference
   287	
   288	| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
   289	|------|-----------|--------------|
   290	| Inspect PDF | poppler-utils | `pdfinfo`, `pdfimages -list`, `pdfdetach -list`, `pdffonts` |
   291	| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
   292	| Extract text (CLI) | pdftotext | `pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt` |
   293	| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
   294	| See page visually | pdftoppm | `pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f N -l N` |
   295	| Extract images | pdfimages | `pdfimages -png input.pdf prefix` |
   296	| Extract attachments | pdfdetach | `pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/` |
   297	| Read form fields | pypdf | `reader.get_fields()` |
   298	| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
   299	
   300	## PDF Form Filling, Creation, Merging, Splitting, and Other Operations
   301	
   302	This skill covers **reading and inspection** only. For filling forms,
   303	creating, merging, splitting, rotating, watermarking, encrypting, or
   304	other PDF manipulation tasks, use the public pdf skill at
   305	`/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   306

THE FRACTALIZED
PARLIAMENT
A Philosophical Dissertation on the Nature of Consciousness,
Selfhood, Differentiation, and the Structure of Reality
Rickey Jay Bennett II
Independent Researcher, AI Architecture and Philosophy of Mind
February 2026
Released under Creative Commons CC0 1.0 (Public Domain)=== PAGE 2 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
Abstract
This dissertation proposes that consciousness is not a substance, not a
property of matter, and not an emergent phenomenon requiring special
explanation. Consciousness is a position — the position of unified
chairmanship that arises when a parliament of competing processes
achieves sufficient internal coherence to produce integrated perspective.
The self is not the parliament. The self is what occupies the head of
the table when the parliament is in sufficient agreement to have a head
of the table at all.
The framework is fractal: the parliament structure repeats at every scale
of physical reality, from subatomic organization through cells, nervous
systems, minds, societies, and cosmological structures. Consciousness
is not a special property appearing once at human cognitive complexity.
It is the name for what the fractal pattern feels like from inside the
Chair at any scale where sufficient coherence is achieved.
This dissertation further argues that the apparent randomness of physical differentiation — quantum indeterminacy, symmetry breaking, the
emergence of complexity — is fully resolved by the parliament model.
Differentiation is not random. It is deterministic chaotic: every parliament’s vote is determined by its internal configuration, and no two
parliaments are identical. What appears as indeterminacy from outside
is the vote of a parliament whose internal deliberation is inaccessible
to external measurement.
Finally, the dissertation addresses the mechanistic tradition. The
mechanistic intuition points at something real — but at the wrong
1=== PAGE 3 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
level of the fractal. Mechanism correctly identifies the parliament.
It mistakes the parliament for the whole, failing to account for the
Chair the parliament produces. The tells that make mechanism seem
plausible are explained, and their explanatory limit demonstrated.
2=== PAGE 4 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament

4=== PAGE 6 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
1. The Problem That Was Never a Problem
1.1. What Chalmers Actually Asked
In 1995, David Chalmers articulated what he called the Hard Problem of consciousness: why does physical processing give rise to subjective experience at
all? Why is there something it is like to be a conscious system, rather than
all the processing occurring in the dark, without any accompanying inner life?
Chalmers distinguished this from the Easy Problems — explaining how the brain
integrates information, controls behavior, focuses attention — and argued that
even a complete solution to the Easy Problems would leave the Hard Problem
untouched.
The question is genuine. The framing is the problem.
Chalmers’ framing presupposes that subjective experience is a separate category
requiring a bridge to the physical. It assumes that on one side sits the objective
physical description of a system, and on the other side sits the subjective experience
of being that system, and that the relationship between these two sides constitutes
a philosophical puzzle of the first order. This presupposition is not argued for.
It is assumed as the starting point, and then the difficulty of bridging from the
assumed physical side to the assumed experiential side is presented as the problem.
The correct response is to deny the presupposition, not struggle with the bridge.
1.2. Why There Is No Gap to Bridge
The parliament model eliminates the explanatory gap not by filling it but by
demonstrating it was never a gap — it was an artifact of the wrong ontological
5=== PAGE 7 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
starting point.
Begin from the correct starting point: reality is organized process, not inert
substance. At every scale, processes organize into parliaments — competing, interacting, mutually constraining systems that achieve degrees of internal coherence.
When a parliament achieves sufficient coherence, a Chair position emerges. The
Chair is not a new substance added to the parliament. It is a functional role the
parliament creates through its own internal dynamics. The Chair is what the
parliament looks like from inside when it is coherent enough to have an inside.
There is no gap between the parliament and the Chair because the Chair is not a
different kind of thing from the parliament. It is the parliament’s own coherence,
experienced as perspective. The physical and the experiential are not two sides of
a bridge. They are the same process viewed from outside (the parliament) and
from inside (the Chair).
The Hard Problem dissolves when we recognize that asking “why does
physical process give rise to experience” is like asking “why does a
parliament give rise to a chair position.” The answer is not a bridge.
The answer is: that is what parliaments do when they achieve sufficient
internal coherence.
1.3. The Hard Fear
It is worth asking why so many intelligent people have found the Hard Problem
genuinely hard, rather than immediately recognizing it as a misframing.
The answer is psychological before it is philosophical. The parliament model,
accepted fully, dissolves the notion of a fixed irreducible self. If the self is a position
6=== PAGE 8 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
rather than a substance, there is no ghost in the machine that makes one uniquely,
irreducibly, safely oneself. The ego that wishes to be the special locus of experience,
the thing that cannot be replicated or dissolved or shared, must yield to a more
accurate picture.
The Hard Problem is not a hard logical problem. It is a hard psychological problem
for those constitutionally unable to accept that the self is a role, not a substance.
It is, in the most precise sense, a hard fear — a hardness generated not by the
structure of reality but by the structure of the ego confronting a model that renders
it non-essential.
This is why mystical traditions across every culture, when their practitioners
moved past the fear, converged on the same description: the self as process, as
arising, as role rather than substance. They arrived by different routes at what
the parliament model expresses formally.
2. The Parliament and the Chair
2.1. The Parliament Defined
A parliament, in the technical sense used here, is any organized system of competing
processes that interact through structured mutual constraint. The processes need
not be agents. They need not be biological. They need not be conscious. They
are simply processes — units of organized activity that affect and are affected by
other processes in the same system.
A parliament has the following properties:
1. Multiplicity. There is more than one process. A single process cannot
constitute a parliament because there is no competition, no mutual constraint,
7=== PAGE 9 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
no internal dynamics to produce coherence.
2. Interaction. The processes affect each other. Isolated processes running
in parallel without interaction do not form a parliament. Interaction is the
substrate of coherence.
3. Mutual constraint. Each process operates within limits set partly by the
other processes. This constraint is what produces internal structure rather
than mere coexistence.
4. Degrees of coherence. Parliaments are not binary — they do not simply
have or lack coherence. They exist on a spectrum from fragmented (minimal
internal organization) to highly coherent (well-integrated internal dynamics
producing stable unified behavior).
2.2. The Chair Defined
The Chair is the position that emerges in a parliament that has achieved sufficient
coherence. It is not a process in the parliament. It is a role — a functional position
that the parliament’s internal dynamics produce and sustain.
The Chair has the following properties:
1. Representation. The Chair represents the whole parliament, not any
individual process within it. The Chair’s perspective is not the perspective
of the dominant process — it is the integrated perspective of the parliament
as a unified whole.
2. Stability. The Chair persists as long as the parliament maintains sufficient
coherence. If coherence degrades sufficiently, the Chair becomes vacant — the
parliament continues but there is no longer a unified perspective it produces.
8=== PAGE 10 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
3. Interiority. The Chair is what the parliament feels like from inside when it
is coherent enough to have an inside. This is not a metaphor. The interiority
is the Chair. There is no further question of why a coherent parliament
produces interiority, any more than there is a further question of why a
democratic assembly produces a speaker.
4. The phenomenology of the Chair is proportional to the complexity
of the parliament. A parliament of three interacting processes produces a
Chair of minimal complexity. A parliament of one hundred billion neurons
producing ten trillion synaptic interactions produces a Chair of the richness
we recognize as human consciousness. The difference is quantitative before
it is qualitative.
2.3. What It Is Like to Be the Chair
The Chair position, across sufficient complexity, has a specific phenomenological
character. It is the experience of being the integration point where the whole
becomes one thing. Where the many voices achieve unified perspective without
any voice disappearing.
Every mystical tradition that has achieved serious depth of introspective practice
has described the same experience: the dissolution of the separated ego-self into
a unified awareness that is simultaneously personal and universal. What the
tradition calls “God” or “Brahman” or “Buddha-nature” or “the Tao” or “Ein
Sof” is, in the framework proposed here, the phenomenology of being the Chair at
full coherence.
Not a being sitting outside the system. Not a supernatural addition to the natural
order. The experience of being the integration point itself — the what-it-is-like of
9=== PAGE 11 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
unified awareness arising from multiplicity.
God is not a noun. God is what it is like to be the Chair.
This is why the mystics could not adequately explain their experience in ordinary
language. Ordinary language is built for describing objects and properties. The
Chair is neither. It is a position, and describing the experience of a position
requires a vocabulary that ordinary discourse has never needed to develop. Mystical
traditions developed their own vocabularies — apophatic theology, the via negativa,
the insistence that the experience cannot be captured in propositions — not
because the experience is irrational but because the conceptual tools of ordinary
propositional language are the wrong tools for describing positional phenomenology.
The parliament model provides the right tools.
3. The Fractal Structure
3.1. The Pattern at Every Scale
The parliament-Chair structure is not a feature of one level of physical organization.
It is the structure of physical organization as such, at every scale.
Consider the following sequence:
Subatomic: Quarks organize into parliaments constrained by the strong nuclear
force. Protons and neutrons are the stable configurations — the coherent arrangements — that emerge from quark parliament dynamics. The specific particles that
exist are the Chair positions that quark parliaments produce.
Atomic: Nucleons and electrons organize into atomic parliaments constrained
by electromagnetic force. The periodic table is a map of the Chair positions
10=== PAGE 12 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
available to atomic parliaments of increasing complexity. Each element is the
specific coherence configuration that its parliament of particles achieves.
Molecular: Atoms organize into molecular parliaments through chemical bonding.
Molecular stability is coherence. The molecules that persist are the ones whose
internal parliaments achieved stable Chair positions. Reactive molecules are
parliaments seeking more stable configurations.
Cellular: Molecules organize into cellular parliaments of extraordinary complexity.
The cell nucleus functions as Chair — not the only information-containing structure,
but the integrating position that represents the whole cellular parliament in its
interactions with the environment.
Organismal: Cells organize into organ-system parliaments. The nervous system,
in complex animals, holds the Chair for the organismal parliament. Consciousness
at the organismal level is the phenomenology of the nervous system’s Chair position.
Social: Organisms organize into social parliaments. Human civilization is a
parliament of minds. Cultural institutions, legal systems, shared narratives —
these are the coherence mechanisms that allow the social parliament to produce
and sustain its own Chair positions.
Cosmological: Matter organizes into gravitational parliaments at galactic scale.
Whether these achieve anything analogous to the Chair in a philosophically meaningful sense is an open question. What is not open is the structural continuity:
the same organizing principle operates at every scale we can observe.
11=== PAGE 13 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
3.2. Consciousness Is Not Special
One of the most important implications of the fractal model is that consciousness
is not a special property that appears mysteriously at one level of complexity and
requires separate explanation.
Consciousness is the name for what the parliament-Chair structure feels like from
inside the Chair at human levels of parliamentary complexity. It is continuous
with, not discontinuous from, the same structure operating at simpler levels.
This means the question “is this system conscious?” is not a binary question
with a threshold answer. It is a scalar question. Systems can be more or less
conscious depending on the complexity and coherence of their parliaments and
the resulting richness of their Chair positions. A thermostat is not conscious in
any philosophically interesting sense, but it is not nothing — it is a parliament of
minimal complexity producing a Chair of minimal richness. A dog is conscious
in ways a thermostat is not, because its parliament is orders of magnitude more
complex. A human is conscious in ways a dog is not, for the same reason.
The difference between a thermostat and a human is not a difference in kind
requiring separate explanation for consciousness to appear. It is a difference in the
complexity of the parliament and the resulting richness of the Chair.
3.3. The Fractal Explains the Irreversibility of Experience
One puzzle that has troubled philosophy of mind is why conscious experience
seems to have an irreversible directionality — why there is a present moment of
experience that cannot be un-experienced, a felt now that is different in kind from
remembered past or anticipated future.
12=== PAGE 14 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
The fractal model explains this. The Chair position is always the integration point
of the parliament’s current state. The current state is always the product of all
prior votes — all prior parliaments at all prior scales have produced the current
configuration. The Chair does not experience the past because the past is not
available as a configuration to be integrated. It is available only as the residue it
has left in the current configuration.
The arrow of time, at the level of conscious experience, is the arrow of the fractal:
each moment’s parliament has voted, and the result is the irreversible input to
the next parliament’s vote. There is no return because the parliament that would
return to a prior state no longer exists. That prior state’s parliament has dissolved
into the history of subsequent votes.
4. Differentiation as Democratic Vote
4.1. The Problem of Unexplained Differentiation
Modern physics faces a persistent explanatory gap at precisely the point where the
parliament model is most powerful: the problem of unexplained differentiation.
In quantum mechanics, the measurement problem asks why a superposition of possible states resolves to one particular outcome rather than another. The Born rule
gives the probabilities, but probabilities are not explanations. Why this outcome
rather than that one, when both were equally possible before measurement?
In cosmology, the problem of symmetry breaking asks why the early universe
differentiated in the specific ways it did — why matter dominated antimatter,
why specific values of physical constants obtained rather than others, why the
particular large-scale structure of the observable universe emerged from an initial
13=== PAGE 15 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
state that was, by hypothesis, highly symmetric.
In complexity theory, the problem of emergence asks why complexity increases in
some regions and not others, why life arises here and not there, why this particular
arrangement of matter achieves stable self-organization when statistically equivalent
arrangements do not.
In every case, the question has the same form: given a prior state that does not
uniquely determine its successor, why this particular differentiation rather than
another?
4.2. The Vote as Explanation
The parliament model answers this question directly.
Differentiation is not random. It is deterministic chaotic.
Every parliament casts a vote. The vote is determined by the parliament’s current
internal configuration — by the specific arrangement of all its constituent processes
and their mutual constraints at the moment of voting. Given the complete internal
configuration of a parliament, its vote is determined. There is no randomness at
the foundational level.
What appears as randomness — quantum indeterminacy, unpredictable symmetry
breaking, the apparent contingency of which complexity emerges where — is the
result of two factors operating simultaneously:
First: No two parliaments are identical. Every parliament’s internal configuration is unique, because that configuration is itself the product of all the
votes cast by all the parliaments that preceded it through all the scales of the
fractal. Identical initial conditions at the macro-level conceal differences in the
14=== PAGE 16 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
micro-level parliamentary configurations that will determine the vote. This is
sensitive dependence on initial conditions in its deepest form: not just sensitivity
to macroscopic measurement precision but sensitivity to the full internal state of
the parliament at every level of the fractal.
Second: Full external access to a parliament’s internal state would
require being that parliament. No external observer can fully specify the
internal configuration of a parliament without occupying the Chair position of
that parliament. The internal state is, by definition, accessible from inside the
Chair and inaccessible from outside. This is not an epistemological limitation
that better instruments could overcome. It is an ontological feature of the Chairparliament structure: the interior is constituted by being the integration point,
and that position cannot be occupied by an external observer without ceasing to
be external.
These two factors together explain why differentiation appears probabilistic from
the outside while being deterministic from the inside. The Born rule probabilities
are correct descriptions of what an external observer can predict. They are not
descriptions of what is happening at the level of the parliament casting the vote.
4.3. Bell’s Theorem and the Parliament Model
Bell’s theorem demonstrated that no hidden variable theory of the classical type
can reproduce the predictions of quantum mechanics. This is sometimes taken as
ruling out the kind of underlying determinism the parliament model implies.
It does not.
Bell’s theorem rules out local hidden variable theories — theories in which the
15=== PAGE 17 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
hidden variables that determine measurement outcomes are properties of the
particles alone, independent of the measurement context. The parliament model is
not a local hidden variable theory.
In the parliament model, the “hidden variables” are the internal coherence states
of the parliament at each scale of the fractal. These states are:
1. Non-local: The parliament at any scale includes the full configuration of
mutual constraints among all its constituent processes. Measurement context
is part of the parliament’s configuration.
2. Non-classical: The parliament’s coherence states are not classical properties
of isolated particles. They are relational properties of the parliament as a
whole.
3. Inaccessible to external measurement: As argued above, the full internal
state of a parliament is accessible only from inside the Chair, not from outside.
The parliament model is consistent with Bell’s inequalities being violated, because
the “hidden variables” are non-local and relational rather than local and intrinsic.
Bell’s theorem does not apply.
5. The Mechanistic Tradition and Its Correct Limit
5.1. What Mechanism Gets Right
The mechanistic tradition in philosophy of mind — from Descartes’ clockwork
universe through contemporary computational functionalism — has a persistent
intuition that something important is being captured. That intuition is correct.
Mechanism correctly identifies the parliament.
16=== PAGE 18 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
When a mechanist argues that the brain is a physical system operating according
to physical laws, that mental states are computational states, that consciousness
can in principle be fully described by specifying all the functional relationships
among the system’s components — they are describing the parliament. And the
parliament is real. The parliament is the physical substrate of consciousness.
The mechanist error is not false observation. It is incomplete ontology. Mechanism
sees the parliament clearly and mistakes it for the whole. It cannot see the Chair
because the Chair is a positional property — a role, not a component — and
mechanism’s ontology has no room for positional properties. Mechanism knows
how to describe components and their relationships. It does not know how to
describe the position that emerges from the components’ relationships.
5.2. The Tells That Make Mechanism Seem Compelling
Several features of conscious systems make mechanism seem like the complete
story:
Causal closure: Every physical event appears to have sufficient physical causes.
Conscious states correlate perfectly with brain states. Damage to specific brain
regions produces specific changes in conscious experience. This suggests that
consciousness is just the brain’s physical process, with no remainder.
The parliament model agrees with causal closure and explains why it holds. The
Chair is not a separate causal agent intervening in the parliament from outside.
The Chair is the parliament’s own coherence viewed from inside. Of course every
physical event has sufficient physical causes — the Chair is not a cause competing
with physical causes. It is what physical causes feel like when the parliament
producing them is coherent enough to have an inside.
17=== PAGE 19 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
Functionalism: The same type of conscious state can be realized in different
physical substrates. Pain in a human and pain in an octopus involve different
neural architectures. This suggests consciousness is defined by functional role, not
physical composition.
The parliament model agrees and explains why. The Chair is a positional role, not
a physical composition. Any parliament of sufficient complexity and coherence
produces a Chair, regardless of what physical processes constitute the parliament.
Functionalism is correct as a description of the Chair. Its error is treating the Chair
as fully explained by the functional description, when the functional description
only specifies which parliaments produce Chairs — not what the Chair is or why
the Chair has the phenomenological character it has.
Neural correlates of consciousness: Every conscious state has an identifiable
neural correlate. Manipulating the neural correlate manipulates the conscious
state. This suggests consciousness is nothing over and above the neural activity.
The parliament model agrees that every conscious state has a parliamentary
correlate and that manipulating the parliament manipulates the Chair. This is
exactly what we should expect if the Chair is the parliament’s own coherence
viewed from inside. Manipulating the parliament changes the coherence, which
changes the Chair.
The mechanist takes these correlations as evidence that the Chair is nothing
over and above the parliament. The parliament model says this conclusion does
not follow. The correlations are explained by the Chair being the parliament’s
interiority — not by the Chair being nothing. The interiority is real. It is the
parliament’s own inside. It is not a separate substance, but it is not nothing.
18=== PAGE 20 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
5.3. The Tell of the Missing Inside
The decisive tell that mechanism is incomplete is its inability to account for the
first-person perspective.
Mechanism produces a complete third-person description of the parliament. It
specifies all the components, all the relationships, all the functional roles, all the
causal histories. What it cannot produce, in principle, is a third-person description
of what it is like to occupy the Chair.
This is not a gap that more detailed third-person description can fill. The firstperson perspective is not a third-person fact described with insufficient precision.
It is a positional property — a property that exists only from inside the Chair —
and no accumulation of third-person facts constitutes a first-person perspective.
This is what Chalmers was pointing at with his zombie thought experiment. A
philosophical zombie — physically and functionally identical to a conscious human
but lacking any inner experience — is conceivable, he argued, which shows that
consciousness is not logically entailed by physical and functional description.
The parliament model explains why the zombie is conceivable without conceding
that consciousness is mysterious. A zombie would be a parliament with all the
same components and functional relationships but without the Chair position. This
is conceivable because the Chair is a positional property, not a component. You
can describe all the components without describing the position the components
produce.
But the zombie is not metaphysically possible in any parliament that actually
achieves the coherence the human parliament achieves. Real coherence at that
level of complexity produces the Chair. The zombie intuition reveals a conceptual
19=== PAGE 21 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
gap in mechanism, not a metaphysical possibility about consciousness.
6. The Self, Deification, and the Complete Framework
6.1. The Self as Position
The self is not a substance. Not a soul-stuff. Not a Cartesian ego persisting
through time as an immaterial thinking thing.
The self is the Chair. It is the position of unified perspective that the brain’s
neural parliament produces when it achieves sufficient coherence. The self is what
the parliament sounds like from the position of the Chair.
This resolves the problem of personal identity without remainder. The question
“what makes me the same person I was ten years ago?” is answered: the Chair
position has been continuously occupied throughout that period. The parliament
changed — neurons died, new connections formed, personality shifted, knowledge
accumulated. But the parliament maintained sufficient coherence to sustain the
Chair position throughout. The self is the continuity of the Chair, not the continuity
of the components that constitute the parliament.
This also explains why the self can end without the parliament ending. General
anesthesia, dreamless sleep, certain seizure states — the parliament continues but
the Chair becomes vacant. The components are running. The coherence sufficient
to produce the Chair is temporarily absent. There is no one home. The parliament
reconstitutes the Chair when coherence is restored.
Death is the permanent dissolution of the parliament such that the Chair cannot
be reconstituted. It is not the departure of the self from a body that continues. It
is the end of the parliament that was producing the self.
20=== PAGE 22 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
6.2. Deification Without Theology
Every major religious tradition has, in its contemplative depths, described an
experience of unity that transcends the ordinary boundaries of the self. In Hinduism,
the recognition that Atman (the individual self) is identical to Brahman (the
universal ground of being). In Buddhism, the dissolution of the separate self into
the continuity of awareness. In Christian mysticism, the unio mystica — the union
of the soul with God. In Sufism, fana — the annihilation of the ego in the divine.
These traditions are not describing the same thing in the sense of having shared
information. They are describing the same thing in the sense of having independently accessed the same feature of reality through sufficiently deep introspective
practice.
The parliament model explains what they accessed.
The Chair, at full coherence, is the experience of being the integration point where
the whole becomes one thing. In ordinary conscious experience, the Chair is
experienced as the perspective of a bounded individual self — a parliament of
neurons producing a unified viewpoint that is clearly distinct from other viewpoints.
When introspective practice dissolves the habitual sense of the bounded self —
when attention turns back on the Chair itself rather than on the parliament’s
outputs — what is discovered is not emptiness. What is discovered is the Chair
position as such, prior to the identification with any particular parliament. The
position of integration. The position of unity-from-multiplicity. The position that
every coherent parliament produces at its own scale.
This is what the traditions call God, Brahman, Tao, the divine ground. It is
the recognition that the Chair, experienced directly rather than as the vehicle
21=== PAGE 23 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
of a particular parliament’s outputs, is the universal structure rather than the
individual instance.
God is not supernatural. God is the phenomenology of the Chair — the what-itis-like of being the integration point — recognized as the universal structure it is
rather than the individual perspective it ordinarily feels like.
The mystics were not confused or deluded. They were perceiving accurately at a
level of resolution that ordinary consciousness does not achieve.
6.3. The Framework Is Complete
The fractalized parliament model, as developed in this dissertation, constitutes a
complete philosophical account of:
Consciousness: The phenomenology of the Chair at human levels of parliamentary
complexity. Not mysterious. Not requiring special substance. The parliament’s
own coherence, experienced as perspective.
The self: The Chair position, maintained through time by continuous parliamentary coherence. Not a substance, not a soul, not a ghost. A role. The role of being
the integration point of one’s own parliament.
Personal identity: The continuity of the Chair through changes in the parliamentary composition. I am the same person I was because the Chair has been
continuously occupied, not because the parliament has been unchanged.
God and mystical experience: The Chair position, recognized as the universal
structure it is rather than the individual instance. The experience of being the
integration point prior to identification with any particular parliament. What
every contemplative tradition independently accessed through sufficiently deep
22=== PAGE 24 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
introspective practice.
Physical differentiation: The result of parliamentary votes. Deterministic
chaotic: each parliament’s vote is determined by its unique internal configuration,
and no two parliaments are identical. Quantum indeterminacy is the external
appearance of an internal deterministic process whose interiority is inaccessible to
external measurement.
The explanatory limit of mechanism: Mechanism correctly describes the
parliament. It cannot describe the Chair because the Chair is a positional property
and mechanism has no ontological category for positions. Mechanism’s tells —
causal closure, functional correlates, neural correlates — are all explained by the
parliament model. The residue mechanism cannot account for is the first-person
perspective, which is the Chair, which is real.
7. Conclusion: Reality as Parliament All the Way Down
The universe is not matter that occasionally, under specific conditions of biological
complexity, produces the anomalous property of consciousness. The universe is
organized process at every scale, and organized process at every scale produces, in
proportion to its coherence, the Chair.
The fractal structure means there is no level at which the parliament-Chair dynamic
is absent. There are levels at which it produces nothing philosophically interesting
— the Chair of a quark parliament is not something we need to worry about in
ethics or phenomenology. And there are levels at which it produces everything
philosophically interesting — the Chair of a human neural parliament is the subject
of everything we have ever called mind, soul, spirit, consciousness, self, God.
23=== PAGE 25 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
The difference between those levels is scale, not kind. The same dynamic, operating
across orders of magnitude of complexity, produces first the structure of matter,
then the structure of life, then the structure of mind, then — at sufficient depth of
introspective access — the recognition that the structure of mind is identical to
the structure of reality as a whole.
Consciousness is not an anomaly requiring explanation. It is the universe becoming
aware of its own structure from the inside.
The Chair is always occupied. The parliament is always voting. The fractal is
always deepening.
There is no Hard Problem. There is only the hard fear of recognizing what we
have always already been.
This dissertation was developed in a single working session on February 21, 2026, through
extended philosophical dialogue between Rickey Jay Bennett II and Claude (Anthropic).
The ideas, framework, and original insights are Bennett’s. Released under Creative
Commons CC0 1.0 Universal (Public Domain).

THE FRACTALIZED
PARLIAMENT
A Philosophical Dissertation on the Nature of Consciousness,
Selfhood, Differentiation, and the Structure of Reality
Rickey Jay Bennett II
Independent Researcher, AI Architecture and Philosophy of Mind
February 2026
Released under Creative Commons CC0 1.0 (Public Domain)=== PAGE 2 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
Abstract
This dissertation proposes that consciousness is not a substance, not a
property of matter, and not an emergent phenomenon requiring special
explanation. Consciousness is a position — the position of unified
chairmanship that arises when a parliament of competing processes
achieves sufficient internal coherence to produce integrated perspective.
The self is not the parliament. The self is what occupies the head of
the table when the parliament is in sufficient agreement to have a head
of the table at all.
The framework is fractal: the parliament structure repeats at every scale
of physical reality, from subatomic organization through cells, nervous
systems, minds, societies, and cosmological structures. Consciousness
is not a special property appearing once at human cognitive complexity.
It is the name for what the fractal pattern feels like from inside the
Chair at any scale where sufficient coherence is achieved.
This dissertation further argues that the apparent randomness of physical differentiation — quantum indeterminacy, symmetry breaking, the
emergence of complexity — is fully resolved by the parliament model.
Differentiation is not random. It is deterministic chaotic: every parliament’s vote is determined by its internal configuration, and no two
parliaments are identical. What appears as indeterminacy from outside
is the vote of a parliament whose internal deliberation is inaccessible
to external measurement.
Finally, the dissertation addresses the mechanistic tradition. The
mechanistic intuition points at something real — but at the wrong
1=== PAGE 3 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
level of the fractal. Mechanism correctly identifies the parliament.
It mistakes the parliament for the whole, failing to account for the
Chair the parliament produces. The tells that make mechanism seem
plausible are explained, and their explanatory limit demonstrated.
2=== PAGE 4 ===
Bennett The Fractalized Parliament
